Note that here the month may refer either to a month of the {{ill|Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|ja|旧暦|1=Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|1=Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|11=Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|qq=}} or to a [[:en:Solar term|Solar term]] (from [[:en:Liqiu|Start of Autumn]] until the day before [[:en:Bailu (solar term)|White Dew]]).
== Days of Yang Metal Monkey ==
On Kōshin days, a Kōshin Vigil ({{ill|Kōshin Vigil|ja|庚申待|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōshin Vigil|qq=|1=Kōshin-machi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11486004}}, also known as {{ill|Kōshin Lecture|ja|庚申講|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōshin Lecture|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 庚申待|1=Kōshin-machi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11486004}}) was held. {{main|[[:en:Kōshin|Kōshin Faith]]|qq=}}
A Kōshin day is also the [[:en:Ennichi|Festival Day]] of [[:en:Śakra (Buddhism)|Taishakuten]].
=== Choosing a Day === Kōshin days occur on the sixth day (excluding intercalary days {{ill|Intercalary Day|ja|間日|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Intercalary Day|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) of the {{ill|Hassen|ja|八専|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hassen|qq=}} cycle. == See Also == * {{prefix|qq=}} * {{intitle|qq=}}

{{nihongo|'''''Kōshin'''''|庚申|1=Kōshin|lt=Yang Metal Monkey|2=ja|3=庚申|4=zh|5=庚申|6=ko|7=경신|lt_ko=경신|8=fr|9=Singe de métal|10=de|11=Metall-Affe||qq=}} or {{nihongo|''Kōshin-shinkō''|庚申信仰||qq=}} is a folk belief in [[:en:Japan|Japan]] with [[Taoism|Taoist]] origins, influenced by [[Shinto]], [[:en:Buddhism|Buddhism]] and other local beliefs.
An event related to the belief is called {{nihongo|Kōshin-kō|庚申講||qq=}}, held on the Kōshin days that occur every 60 days in accordance with the [[:en:Chinese sexagenary cycle|Chinese sexagenary cycle]]. On this day some believers stay awake to prevent {{nihongo|Sanshi|三尸||qq=}}, entities believed to live inside the bodies of believers, from leaving during that night in order to report the deeds of believers to the god Tentei.
It is not known when this belief arrived in Japan, but it was widespread among the nobles of the imperial court by some time in the 9th century. The Japanese monk [[:en:Ennin|Ennin]], visiting [[:en:Tang dynasty|Tang China]] in 838, wrote that "This night no one sleeps. It is the same as New Year's Eve and the nights of ''Kōshin'' in our country."<ref>{{Cite book |last= |first= |url=http://archive.org/details/diaryrecordofpil0000enni |title=Ennin's Diary. The Record of a Pilgrimage to China in Search of the Law |title-link= |publisher=Ronald Press Company |year=1955 |location=New York |page=58 |translator-last=Reischauer |translator-first=Edwin O. |translator-link=Edwin O. Reischauer|qq=}}</ref> In the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]], [[:en:Bhikkhu|Buddhist monks]] started to write about Kōshin and spread the belief to a wider public. Numerous monuments or pillars called {{nihongo|Kōshin-tō|庚申塔||qq=}} (or also {{nihongo|Kōshin-zuka|庚申塚||qq=}}) were erected all over the country, and the belief remained very popular during the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. However, after the Meiji government issued the [[Shinbutsu bunri|Shinto and Buddhism Separation Order]] in 1872, Kōshin and other folk beliefs were officially rejected as superstitions.
Belief in Kōshin survives, although it is far less popular than it once was. Many Kōshin-tō have been moved inside Buddhist temples or private homes, but many remain alongside roads and there are still some well-maintained {{nihongo|Kōshin-dō|Kōshin-dō||qq=}} (Kōshin halls) either attached to Buddhist temples or standing alone.
==Deities and customs== The most ancient Kōshin custom is that of staying awake one special night every sixty days. This night is called ''Kōshin-Machi'' (庚申待 - Kōshin Waiting).
The main Kōshin belief is the concept that [[:en:Three Corpses|Three Corpses]], or ''Sanshi'' (三尸), live in every human body. The Sanshi keep track of the deeds of the person they inhabit. On the night called Kōshin-Machi, the ''Sanshis'' leave the body and go to [[:en:King of Heavens|Tentei]] (天帝), the Heavenly God, to report the deeds of that person. Tentei then punishes bad people, making them ill, shortening their lifespans or, in extreme cases, ending their lives. Believers in Kōshin try to live without performing bad deeds, but those who believe that they have reason to fear try to stay awake during Kōshin nights, as the only way to prevent the Sanshi from reporting to Tentei.
In the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]], Kōshin-Machi became more popular among commoners, leading to a proliferation of festivities and cultic activities. Many of these practices centered on the worship of specific deities. These deities were visualized in [[:en:Hanging scroll|Hanging scroll]]s, icons, and stone carvings, many of which continue to dot the rural landscape of Japan today. One specially prominent god in the Kōshin cult was [[Shōmen-Kongō]] (Blue-Faced [[:en:Vajra-Yakṣa|Vajra-Yakṣa]]), a fearsome deity with many arms. The first scriptures that established his connection with Kōshin were produced in the context of esoteric Buddhist rituals performed at the temple known as {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Onjōji|Onjōji]]|qq=}} or {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Miidera|Miidera]]|qq=}}. Another temple crucial in the early development of this cult was [[Shitennō-ji]]. Shōmen-Kongō became Kōshin-san when people expected this deity to make the Sanshis themselves ill and prevent them from going to Tentei.

It is the 57th combination in the Sexagenary cycle comprehensive, preceded by {{ill|Kimi|ja|1=Yin Earth Goat|2=ja|己未|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} and followed by {{ill|Shinyuu|ja|1=Yin Metal Rooster|2=ja|辛酉|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinyuu|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. In {{ill|Yin-Yang Five Elements|ja|陰陽五行|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yin-Yang Five Elements|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 陰陽五行思想|1=yin-yang wu xing theory|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11265234}}, the stem {{ill|Geng|ja|庚|1=Kanoe (庚)|lt=Kanoe (庚)|2=ja|3=庚|4=zh|5=庚|1=Kanoe (庚)|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Geng|13=User:Immanuelle/Kanoe (庚)|qq=}} of the [[:en:Heavenly Stems|Ten Heavenly Stems]] represents Yang Metal, and the branch [[:en:Monkey (zodiac)|Monkey (申)]] of the [[:en:Earthly Branches|Twelve Earthly Branches]] also represents Yang Metal, a state referred to as {{ill|Bihwa|ja|五行思想#比和（ひわ）|1=Wu Xing|1=Wuxing (Chinese philosophy)#Harmonious Relationship (比和)|2=ja|3=五行思想#比和（ひわ）|lt=Harmonious Relationship (Five Elements)|qq=Bihwa|lt_ja=比和|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bihwa|13=User:Immanuelle/比和|qq=|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q218652}}.
==Pronunciation== * English: Yang Metal Monkey (庚申) ** Chinese (Mandarin Pinyin): gēngshēn ** Cantonese (Jyutping): gaang1 san1 ** Japanese: ***Kunyomi 1: Kanoe-saru ***Kunyomi 2: koukin-no-saru ***Onyomi 1: koushin ** Korean (Revised Romanization, Hangul): gyeongsin (경신) ** Vietnamese (Hán-Việt): Canh Thân
== Years of Yang Metal Monkey == [[:en:Common Era|Common Era]] and [[:en:Japanese imperial year|Imperial Era]] designate years that are multiples of 60 as [[:en:Year|Year]] of Kōshin.
=== Nature and Era Change === Because both the heavenly stem and earthly branch of Kōshin are of [[:en:Metal|Metal]] nature, it was believed that the metal energy pervading the universe in a Kōshin year or day would render human hearts cold and unfeeling. The following combination, {{ill|Shinyuu|ja|1=Yin Metal Rooster|2=ja|辛酉|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinyuu|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, also being metal in nature—with Xin being of Yin energy—was thought to intensify this coldness. Consequently, Kōshin and Shinyuu were considered harbingers of political upheaval, and to avert such changes it was not uncommon to change eras for two consecutive years. For example, this occurred in the first years of [[:en:Man'en|Man'en]] ([[:en:1860|1860]]) and [[:en:Bunkyū|Bunkyu]] ([[:en:1861|1861]]).

Many Kōshin-tō have been moved inside Buddhist temples or private homes, but many remain alongside roads and there are still some well-maintained {{nihongo|Kōshin-dō|Kōshin-dō||qq=}} (Kōshin halls) either attached to Buddhist temples or standing alone.
==Deities and customs== The most ancient Kōshin custom is that of staying awake one special night every sixty days. This night is called ''Kōshin-Machi'' (庚申待 - Kōshin Waiting).
The main Kōshin belief is the concept that [[:en:Three Corpses|Three Corpses]], or ''Sanshi'' (三尸), live in every human body. The Sanshi keep track of the deeds of the person they inhabit. On the night called Kōshin-Machi, the ''Sanshis'' leave the body and go to [[:en:King of Heavens|Tentei]] (天帝), the Heavenly God, to report the deeds of that person. Tentei then punishes bad people, making them ill, shortening their lifespans or, in extreme cases, ending their lives. Believers in Kōshin try to live without performing bad deeds, but those who believe that they have reason to fear try to stay awake during Kōshin nights, as the only way to prevent the Sanshi from reporting to Tentei.
In the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]], Kōshin-Machi became more popular among commoners, leading to a proliferation of festivities and cultic activities. Many of these practices centered on the worship of specific deities. These deities were visualized in [[:en:Hanging scroll|Hanging scroll]]s, icons, and stone carvings, many of which continue to dot the rural landscape of Japan today. One specially prominent god in the Kōshin cult was [[Shōmen-Kongō]] (Blue-Faced [[:en:Vajra-Yakṣa|Vajra-Yakṣa]]), a fearsome deity with many arms. The first scriptures that established his connection with Kōshin were produced in the context of esoteric Buddhist rituals performed at the temple known as {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Onjōji|Onjōji]]|qq=}} or {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Miidera|Miidera]]|qq=}}. Another temple crucial in the early development of this cult was [[Shitennō-ji]]. Shōmen-Kongō became Kōshin-san when people expected this deity to make the Sanshis themselves ill and prevent them from going to Tentei.

{{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q3082157]] Wikidata name: Kōshin [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 07:49, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{infobox Chinese|l=Yang Metal Monkey|kanji=庚申|romaji=kanoe saru|onyomi=kōshin|p=gēngshēn|w=keng-shen|mi=kɤŋ⁵³ ʂən|y=geng1 san1|j=geng1 san1|ci=kɪŋ ʂɐn|mc=kæŋ ʂin|oc-bs=kˤraŋ ʂin|qq=}} {{otheruses|Sexagenary cycle|日本人の信仰対象|庚申信仰|qq=}} {{merge|1=Kōshin|qq=}} Might be worth moving to or merging with {{ill|Kōshin|ja|こうしん|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōshin|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} {{afc comment|1=This one is really weird with a potential wikidata conflict[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 19:32, 10 November 2025 (UTC)}} {{Sexagenary cycle comprehensive|qq=}} '''Yang Metal Monkey also known as Kōshin''' (庚申; かのえさる、こうきんのさる、こうしん) is one of the [[:en:Sexagenary cycle|Sexagenary cycle]].
It is the 57th combination in the Sexagenary cycle comprehensive, preceded by {{ill|Kimi|ja|1=Yin Earth Goat|2=ja|己未|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} and followed by {{ill|Shinyuu|ja|1=Yin Metal Rooster|2=ja|辛酉|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinyuu|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. In {{ill|Yin-Yang Five Elements|ja|陰陽五行|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yin-Yang Five Elements|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 陰陽五行思想|1=yin-yang wu xing theory|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11265234}}, the stem {{ill|Geng|ja|庚|1=Kanoe (庚)|lt=Kanoe (庚)|2=ja|3=庚|4=zh|5=庚|1=Kanoe (庚)|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Geng|13=User:Immanuelle/Kanoe (庚)|qq=}} of the [[:en:Heavenly Stems|Ten Heavenly Stems]] represents Yang Metal, and the branch [[:en:Monkey (zodiac)|Monkey (申)]] of the [[:en:Earthly Branches|Twelve Earthly Branches]] also represents Yang Metal, a state referred to as {{ill|Bihwa|ja|五行思想#比和（ひわ）|1=Wu Xing|1=Wuxing (Chinese philosophy)#Harmonious Relationship (比和)|2=ja|3=五行思想#比和（ひわ）|lt=Harmonious Relationship (Five Elements)|qq=Bihwa|lt_ja=比和|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bihwa|13=User:Immanuelle/比和|qq=|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q218652}}.
==Pronunciation== * English: Yang Metal Monkey (庚申) ** Chinese (Mandarin Pinyin): gēngshēn ** Cantonese (Jyutping): gaang1 san1 ** Japanese: ***Kunyomi 1: Kanoe-saru ***Kunyomi 2: koukin-no-saru ***Onyomi 1: koushin ** Korean (Revised Romanization, Hangul): gyeongsin (경신) ** Vietnamese (Hán-Việt): Canh Thân
== Years of Yang Metal Monkey == [[:en:Common Era|Common Era]] and [[:en:Japanese imperial year|Imperial Era]] designate years that are multiples of 60 as [[:en:Year|Year]] of Kōshin.
=== Nature and Era Change === Because both the heavenly stem and earthly branch of Kōshin are of [[:en:Metal|Metal]] nature, it was believed that the metal energy pervading the universe in a Kōshin year or day would render human hearts cold and unfeeling. The following combination, {{ill|Shinyuu|ja|1=Yin Metal Rooster|2=ja|辛酉|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinyuu|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, also being metal in nature—with Xin being of Yin energy—was thought to intensify this coldness. Consequently, Kōshin and Shinyuu were considered harbingers of political upheaval, and to avert such changes it was not uncommon to change eras for two consecutive years. For example, this occurred in the first years of [[:en:Man'en|Man'en]] ([[:en:1860|1860]]) and [[:en:Bunkyū|Bunkyu]] ([[:en:1861|1861]]).

== Months of Yang Metal Monkey == In years where the last digit of the Western Calendar year is 3 or 8 (when the heavenly stem is {{ill|Guǐ|ja|癸|1=Mizunoto (癸)|lt=Mizunoto (癸)|2=ja|3=癸|4=zh|5=癸|1=Mizunoto (癸)|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Guǐ|13=User:Immanuelle/Mizunoto (癸)|qq=}} or {{ill|Wu|ja|戊|1=Tsuchinoe (戊)|lt=Tsuchinoe (戊)|2=ja|3=戊|4=zh|5=戊|1=Tsuchinoe (戊)|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Wu|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsuchinoe (戊)|qq=}}), the month of [[:en:July|July]] becomes the Kōshin [[:en:Month|Month (Calendar)]]. Note that here the month may refer either to a month of the {{ill|Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|ja|旧暦|1=Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|1=Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|11=Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|qq=}} or to a [[:en:Solar term|Solar term]] (from [[:en:Liqiu|Start of Autumn]] until the day before [[:en:Bailu (solar term)|White Dew]]).
== Days of Yang Metal Monkey ==
On Kōshin days, a Kōshin Vigil ({{ill|Kōshin Vigil|ja|庚申待|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōshin Vigil|qq=|1=Kōshin-machi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11486004}}, also known as {{ill|Kōshin Lecture|ja|庚申講|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōshin Lecture|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 庚申待|1=Kōshin-machi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11486004}}) was held. {{main|[[:en:Kōshin|Kōshin Faith]]|qq=}}
A Kōshin day is also the [[:en:Ennichi|Festival Day]] of [[:en:Śakra (Buddhism)|Taishakuten]].
=== Choosing a Day === Kōshin days occur on the sixth day (excluding intercalary days {{ill|Intercalary Day|ja|間日|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Intercalary Day|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) of the {{ill|Hassen|ja|八専|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hassen|qq=}} cycle. == See Also == * {{prefix|qq=}} * {{intitle|qq=}}

{{nihongo|'''''Kōshin'''''|庚申|1=Kōshin|lt=Yang Metal Monkey|2=ja|3=庚申|4=zh|5=庚申|6=ko|7=경신|lt_ko=경신|8=fr|9=Singe de métal|10=de|11=Metall-Affe||qq=}} or {{nihongo|''Kōshin-shinkō''|庚申信仰||qq=}} is a folk belief in [[:en:Japan|Japan]] with [[Taoism|Taoist]] origins, influenced by [[Shinto]], [[:en:Buddhism|Buddhism]] and other local beliefs.
An event related to the belief is called {{nihongo|Kōshin-kō|庚申講||qq=}}, held on the Kōshin days that occur every 60 days in accordance with the [[:en:Chinese sexagenary cycle|Chinese sexagenary cycle]]. On this day some believers stay awake to prevent {{nihongo|Sanshi|三尸||qq=}}, entities believed to live inside the bodies of believers, from leaving during that night in order to report the deeds of believers to the god Tentei.
It is not known when this belief arrived in Japan, but it was widespread among the nobles of the imperial court by some time in the 9th century. The Japanese monk [[:en:Ennin|Ennin]], visiting [[:en:Tang dynasty|Tang China]] in 838, wrote that "This night no one sleeps. It is the same as New Year's Eve and the nights of ''Kōshin'' in our country."<ref>{{Cite book |last= |first= |url=http://archive.org/details/diaryrecordofpil0000enni |title=Ennin's Diary. The Record of a Pilgrimage to China in Search of the Law |title-link= |publisher=Ronald Press Company |year=1955 |location=New York |page=58 |translator-last=Reischauer |translator-first=Edwin O. |translator-link=Edwin O. Reischauer|qq=}}</ref> In the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]], [[:en:Bhikkhu|Buddhist monks]] started to write about Kōshin and spread the belief to a wider public. Numerous monuments or pillars called {{nihongo|Kōshin-tō|庚申塔||qq=}} (or also {{nihongo|Kōshin-zuka|庚申塚||qq=}}) were erected all over the country, and the belief remained very popular during the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. However, after the Meiji government issued the [[Shinbutsu bunri|Shinto and Buddhism Separation Order]] in 1872, Kōshin and other folk beliefs were officially rejected as superstitions.

Many of these practices centered on the worship of specific deities. These deities were visualized in [[:en:Hanging scroll|Hanging scroll]]s, icons, and stone carvings, many of which continue to dot the rural landscape of Japan today. One specially prominent god in the Kōshin cult was [[Shōmen-Kongō]] (Blue-Faced [[:en:Vajra-Yakṣa|Vajra-Yakṣa]]), a fearsome deity with many arms. The first scriptures that established his connection with Kōshin were produced in the context of esoteric Buddhist rituals performed at the temple known as {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Onjōji|Onjōji]]|qq=}} or {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Miidera|Miidera]]|qq=}}. It is the 57th combination in the Sexagenary cycle comprehensive, preceded by {{ill|Kimi|ja|1=Yin Earth Goat|2=ja|己未|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} and followed by {{ill|Shinyuu|ja|1=Yin Metal Rooster|2=ja|辛酉|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinyuu|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. ==Pronunciation== * English: Yang Metal Monkey (庚申) ** Chinese (Mandarin Pinyin): gēngshēn ** Cantonese (Jyutping): gaang1 san1 ** Japanese: ***Kunyomi 1: Kanoe-saru ***Kunyomi 2: koukin-no-saru ***Onyomi 1: koushin ** Korean (Revised Romanization, Hangul): gyeongsin (경신) ** Vietnamese (Hán-Việt): Canh Thân
== Years of Yang Metal Monkey == [[:en:Common Era|Common Era]] and [[:en:Japanese imperial year|Imperial Era]] designate years that are multiples of 60 as [[:en:Year|Year]] of Kōshin.
=== Nature and Era Change === Because both the heavenly stem and earthly branch of Kōshin are of [[:en:Metal|Metal]] nature, it was believed that the metal energy pervading the universe in a Kōshin year or day would render human hearts cold and unfeeling. The following combination, {{ill|Shinyuu|ja|1=Yin Metal Rooster|2=ja|辛酉|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinyuu|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, also being metal in nature—with Xin being of Yin energy—was thought to intensify this coldness. Consequently, Kōshin and Shinyuu were considered harbingers of political upheaval, and to avert such changes it was not uncommon to change eras for two consecutive years. For example, this occurred in the first years of [[:en:Man'en|Man'en]] ([[:en:1860|1860]]) and [[:en:Bunkyū|Bunkyu]] ([[:en:1861|1861]]).

== Months of Yang Metal Monkey == In years where the last digit of the Western Calendar year is 3 or 8 (when the heavenly stem is {{ill|Guǐ|ja|癸|1=Mizunoto (癸)|lt=Mizunoto (癸)|2=ja|3=癸|4=zh|5=癸|1=Mizunoto (癸)|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Guǐ|13=User:Immanuelle/Mizunoto (癸)|qq=}} or {{ill|Wu|ja|戊|1=Tsuchinoe (戊)|lt=Tsuchinoe (戊)|2=ja|3=戊|4=zh|5=戊|1=Tsuchinoe (戊)|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Wu|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsuchinoe (戊)|qq=}}), the month of [[:en:July|July]] becomes the Kōshin [[:en:Month|Month (Calendar)]]. Note that here the month may refer either to a month of the {{ill|Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|ja|旧暦|1=Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|1=Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|11=Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|qq=}} or to a [[:en:Solar term|Solar term]] (from [[:en:Liqiu|Start of Autumn]] until the day before [[:en:Bailu (solar term)|White Dew]]).
== Days of Yang Metal Monkey ==
On Kōshin days, a Kōshin Vigil ({{ill|Kōshin Vigil|ja|庚申待|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōshin Vigil|qq=|1=Kōshin-machi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11486004}}, also known as {{ill|Kōshin Lecture|ja|庚申講|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōshin Lecture|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 庚申待|1=Kōshin-machi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11486004}}) was held. {{main|[[:en:Kōshin|Kōshin Faith]]|qq=}}
A Kōshin day is also the [[:en:Ennichi|Festival Day]] of [[:en:Śakra (Buddhism)|Taishakuten]].
=== Choosing a Day === Kōshin days occur on the sixth day (excluding intercalary days {{ill|Intercalary Day|ja|間日|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Intercalary Day|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) of the {{ill|Hassen|ja|八専|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hassen|qq=}} cycle. == See Also == * {{prefix|qq=}} * {{intitle|qq=}}

{{Short description|Folk religion|qq=}} {{distinguish|Ko-Shintō|qq=}} {{more footnotes|date=August 2020|qq=}} {{Italic title|reason=|qq=}}
{{nihongo|'''''Kōshin'''''|庚申|1=Kōshin|lt=Yang Metal Monkey|2=ja|3=庚申|4=zh|5=庚申|6=ko|7=경신|lt_ko=경신|8=fr|9=Singe de métal|10=de|11=Metall-Affe||qq=}} or {{nihongo|''Kōshin-shinkō''|庚申信仰||qq=}} is a folk belief in [[:en:Japan|Japan]] with [[Taoism|Taoist]] origins, influenced by [[Shinto]], [[:en:Buddhism|Buddhism]] and other local beliefs.
An event related to the belief is called {{nihongo|Kōshin-kō|庚申講||qq=}}, held on the Kōshin days that occur every 60 days in accordance with the [[:en:Chinese sexagenary cycle|Chinese sexagenary cycle]]. On this day some believers stay awake to prevent {{nihongo|Sanshi|三尸||qq=}}, entities believed to live inside the bodies of believers, from leaving during that night in order to report the deeds of believers to the god Tentei.
It is not known when this belief arrived in Japan, but it was widespread among the nobles of the imperial court by some time in the 9th century. The Japanese monk [[:en:Ennin|Ennin]], visiting [[:en:Tang dynasty|Tang China]] in 838, wrote that "This night no one sleeps. It is the same as New Year's Eve and the nights of ''Kōshin'' in our country."<ref>{{Cite book |last= |first= |url=http://archive.org/details/diaryrecordofpil0000enni |title=Ennin's Diary. The Record of a Pilgrimage to China in Search of the Law |title-link= |publisher=Ronald Press Company |year=1955 |location=New York |page=58 |translator-last=Reischauer |translator-first=Edwin O. |translator-link=Edwin O. Reischauer|qq=}}</ref> In the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]], [[:en:Bhikkhu|Buddhist monks]] started to write about Kōshin and spread the belief to a wider public. Numerous monuments or pillars called {{nihongo|Kōshin-tō|庚申塔||qq=}} (or also {{nihongo|Kōshin-zuka|庚申塚||qq=}}) were erected all over the country, and the belief remained very popular during the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. However, after the Meiji government issued the [[Shinbutsu bunri|Shinto and Buddhism Separation Order]] in 1872, Kōshin and other folk beliefs were officially rejected as superstitions.
Belief in Kōshin survives, although it is far less popular than it once was. Many Kōshin-tō have been moved inside Buddhist temples or private homes, but many remain alongside roads and there are still some well-maintained {{nihongo|Kōshin-dō|Kōshin-dō||qq=}} (Kōshin halls) either attached to Buddhist temples or standing alone.
==Deities and customs== The most ancient Kōshin custom is that of staying awake one special night every sixty days. This night is called ''Kōshin-Machi'' (庚申待 - Kōshin Waiting).
The main Kōshin belief is the concept that [[:en:Three Corpses|Three Corpses]], or ''Sanshi'' (三尸), live in every human body. The Sanshi keep track of the deeds of the person they inhabit. On the night called Kōshin-Machi, the ''Sanshis'' leave the body and go to [[:en:King of Heavens|Tentei]] (天帝), the Heavenly God, to report the deeds of that person. Tentei then punishes bad people, making them ill, shortening their lifespans or, in extreme cases, ending their lives. Believers in Kōshin try to live without performing bad deeds, but those who believe that they have reason to fear try to stay awake during Kōshin nights, as the only way to prevent the Sanshi from reporting to Tentei.
In the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]], Kōshin-Machi became more popular among commoners, leading to a proliferation of festivities and cultic activities. Many of these practices centered on the worship of specific deities. These deities were visualized in [[:en:Hanging scroll|Hanging scroll]]s, icons, and stone carvings, many of which continue to dot the rural landscape of Japan today. One specially prominent god in the Kōshin cult was [[Shōmen-Kongō]] (Blue-Faced [[:en:Vajra-Yakṣa|Vajra-Yakṣa]]), a fearsome deity with many arms. The first scriptures that established his connection with Kōshin were produced in the context of esoteric Buddhist rituals performed at the temple known as {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Onjōji|Onjōji]]|qq=}} or {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Miidera|Miidera]]|qq=}}. Another temple crucial in the early development of this cult was [[Shitennō-ji]]. Shōmen-Kongō became Kōshin-san when people expected this deity to make the Sanshis themselves ill and prevent them from going to Tentei.

== Months of Yang Metal Monkey == In years where the last digit of the Western Calendar year is 3 or 8 (when the heavenly stem is {{ill|Guǐ|ja|癸|1=Mizunoto (癸)|lt=Mizunoto (癸)|2=ja|3=癸|4=zh|5=癸|1=Mizunoto (癸)|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Guǐ|13=User:Immanuelle/Mizunoto (癸)|qq=}} or {{ill|Wu|ja|戊|1=Tsuchinoe (戊)|lt=Tsuchinoe (戊)|2=ja|3=戊|4=zh|5=戊|1=Tsuchinoe (戊)|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Wu|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsuchinoe (戊)|qq=}}), the month of [[:en:July|July]] becomes the Kōshin [[:en:Month|Month (Calendar)]]. Note that here the month may refer either to a month of the {{ill|Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|ja|旧暦|1=Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|1=Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|11=Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|qq=}} or to a [[:en:Solar term|Solar term]] (from [[:en:Liqiu|Start of Autumn]] until the day before [[:en:Bailu (solar term)|White Dew]]).
== Days of Yang Metal Monkey ==
On Kōshin days, a Kōshin Vigil ({{ill|Kōshin Vigil|ja|庚申待|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōshin Vigil|qq=|1=Kōshin-machi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11486004}}, also known as {{ill|Kōshin Lecture|ja|庚申講|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōshin Lecture|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 庚申待|1=Kōshin-machi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11486004}}) was held. {{main|[[:en:Kōshin|Kōshin Faith]]|qq=}}
A Kōshin day is also the [[:en:Ennichi|Festival Day]] of [[:en:Śakra (Buddhism)|Taishakuten]].
=== Choosing a Day === Kōshin days occur on the sixth day (excluding intercalary days {{ill|Intercalary Day|ja|間日|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Intercalary Day|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) of the {{ill|Hassen|ja|八専|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hassen|qq=}} cycle. == See Also == * {{prefix|qq=}} * {{intitle|qq=}}

{{nihongo|'''''Kōshin'''''|庚申|1=Kōshin|lt=Yang Metal Monkey|2=ja|3=庚申|4=zh|5=庚申|6=ko|7=경신|lt_ko=경신|8=fr|9=Singe de métal|10=de|11=Metall-Affe||qq=}} or {{nihongo|''Kōshin-shinkō''|庚申信仰||qq=}} is a folk belief in [[:en:Japan|Japan]] with [[Taoism|Taoist]] origins, influenced by [[Shinto]], [[:en:Buddhism|Buddhism]] and other local beliefs.
An event related to the belief is called {{nihongo|Kōshin-kō|庚申講||qq=}}, held on the Kōshin days that occur every 60 days in accordance with the [[:en:Chinese sexagenary cycle|Chinese sexagenary cycle]]. On this day some believers stay awake to prevent {{nihongo|Sanshi|三尸||qq=}}, entities believed to live inside the bodies of believers, from leaving during that night in order to report the deeds of believers to the god Tentei.
It is not known when this belief arrived in Japan, but it was widespread among the nobles of the imperial court by some time in the 9th century. The Japanese monk [[:en:Ennin|Ennin]], visiting [[:en:Tang dynasty|Tang China]] in 838, wrote that "This night no one sleeps. It is the same as New Year's Eve and the nights of ''Kōshin'' in our country."<ref>{{Cite book |last= |first= |url=http://archive.org/details/diaryrecordofpil0000enni |title=Ennin's Diary. The Record of a Pilgrimage to China in Search of the Law |title-link= |publisher=Ronald Press Company |year=1955 |location=New York |page=58 |translator-last=Reischauer |translator-first=Edwin O. |translator-link=Edwin O. Reischauer|qq=}}</ref> In the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]], [[:en:Bhikkhu|Buddhist monks]] started to write about Kōshin and spread the belief to a wider public. Numerous monuments or pillars called {{nihongo|Kōshin-tō|庚申塔||qq=}} (or also {{nihongo|Kōshin-zuka|庚申塚||qq=}}) were erected all over the country, and the belief remained very popular during the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. However, after the Meiji government issued the [[Shinbutsu bunri|Shinto and Buddhism Separation Order]] in 1872, Kōshin and other folk beliefs were officially rejected as superstitions.
Belief in Kōshin survives, although it is far less popular than it once was. Many Kōshin-tō have been moved inside Buddhist temples or private homes, but many remain alongside roads and there are still some well-maintained {{nihongo|Kōshin-dō|Kōshin-dō||qq=}} (Kōshin halls) either attached to Buddhist temples or standing alone.
==Deities and customs== The most ancient Kōshin custom is that of staying awake one special night every sixty days. This night is called ''Kōshin-Machi'' (庚申待 - Kōshin Waiting).
The main Kōshin belief is the concept that [[:en:Three Corpses|Three Corpses]], or ''Sanshi'' (三尸), live in every human body. The Sanshi keep track of the deeds of the person they inhabit. On the night called Kōshin-Machi, the ''Sanshis'' leave the body and go to [[:en:King of Heavens|Tentei]] (天帝), the Heavenly God, to report the deeds of that person. Tentei then punishes bad people, making them ill, shortening their lifespans or, in extreme cases, ending their lives. Believers in Kōshin try to live without performing bad deeds, but those who believe that they have reason to fear try to stay awake during Kōshin nights, as the only way to prevent the Sanshi from reporting to Tentei.
In the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]], Kōshin-Machi became more popular among commoners, leading to a proliferation of festivities and cultic activities. Many of these practices centered on the worship of specific deities. These deities were visualized in [[:en:Hanging scroll|Hanging scroll]]s, icons, and stone carvings, many of which continue to dot the rural landscape of Japan today. One specially prominent god in the Kōshin cult was [[Shōmen-Kongō]] (Blue-Faced [[:en:Vajra-Yakṣa|Vajra-Yakṣa]]), a fearsome deity with many arms. The first scriptures that established his connection with Kōshin were produced in the context of esoteric Buddhist rituals performed at the temple known as {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Onjōji|Onjōji]]|qq=}} or {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Miidera|Miidera]]|qq=}}. Another temple crucial in the early development of this cult was [[Shitennō-ji]]. Shōmen-Kongō became Kōshin-san when people expected this deity to make the Sanshis themselves ill and prevent them from going to Tentei.

== Years of Yang Metal Monkey == [[:en:Common Era|Common Era]] and [[:en:Japanese imperial year|Imperial Era]] designate years that are multiples of 60 as [[:en:Year|Year]] of Kōshin.
=== Nature and Era Change === Because both the heavenly stem and earthly branch of Kōshin are of [[:en:Metal|Metal]] nature, it was believed that the metal energy pervading the universe in a Kōshin year or day would render human hearts cold and unfeeling. The following combination, {{ill|Shinyuu|ja|1=Yin Metal Rooster|2=ja|辛酉|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinyuu|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, also being metal in nature—with Xin being of Yin energy—was thought to intensify this coldness. Consequently, Kōshin and Shinyuu were considered harbingers of political upheaval, and to avert such changes it was not uncommon to change eras for two consecutive years. For example, this occurred in the first years of [[:en:Man'en|Man'en]] ([[:en:1860|1860]]) and [[:en:Bunkyū|Bunkyu]] ([[:en:1861|1861]]).

== Months of Yang Metal Monkey == In years where the last digit of the Western Calendar year is 3 or 8 (when the heavenly stem is {{ill|Guǐ|ja|癸|1=Mizunoto (癸)|lt=Mizunoto (癸)|2=ja|3=癸|4=zh|5=癸|1=Mizunoto (癸)|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Guǐ|13=User:Immanuelle/Mizunoto (癸)|qq=}} or {{ill|Wu|ja|戊|1=Tsuchinoe (戊)|lt=Tsuchinoe (戊)|2=ja|3=戊|4=zh|5=戊|1=Tsuchinoe (戊)|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Wu|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsuchinoe (戊)|qq=}}), the month of [[:en:July|July]] becomes the Kōshin [[:en:Month|Month (Calendar)]]. Note that here the month may refer either to a month of the {{ill|Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|ja|旧暦|1=Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|1=Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|11=Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|qq=}} or to a [[:en:Solar term|Solar term]] (from [[:en:Liqiu|Start of Autumn]] until the day before [[:en:Bailu (solar term)|White Dew]]).
== Days of Yang Metal Monkey ==
On Kōshin days, a Kōshin Vigil ({{ill|Kōshin Vigil|ja|庚申待|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōshin Vigil|qq=|1=Kōshin-machi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11486004}}, also known as {{ill|Kōshin Lecture|ja|庚申講|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōshin Lecture|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 庚申待|1=Kōshin-machi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11486004}}) was held. {{main|[[:en:Kōshin|Kōshin Faith]]|qq=}}
A Kōshin day is also the [[:en:Ennichi|Festival Day]] of [[:en:Śakra (Buddhism)|Taishakuten]].
=== Choosing a Day === Kōshin days occur on the sixth day (excluding intercalary days {{ill|Intercalary Day|ja|間日|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Intercalary Day|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) of the {{ill|Hassen|ja|八専|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hassen|qq=}} cycle. == See Also == * {{prefix|qq=}} * {{intitle|qq=}}

{{nihongo|'''''Kōshin'''''|庚申|1=Kōshin|lt=Yang Metal Monkey|2=ja|3=庚申|4=zh|5=庚申|6=ko|7=경신|lt_ko=경신|8=fr|9=Singe de métal|10=de|11=Metall-Affe||qq=}} or {{nihongo|''Kōshin-shinkō''|庚申信仰||qq=}} is a folk belief in [[:en:Japan|Japan]] with [[Taoism|Taoist]] origins, influenced by [[Shinto]], [[:en:Buddhism|Buddhism]] and other local beliefs.
An event related to the belief is called {{nihongo|Kōshin-kō|庚申講||qq=}}, held on the Kōshin days that occur every 60 days in accordance with the [[:en:Chinese sexagenary cycle|Chinese sexagenary cycle]]. On this day some believers stay awake to prevent {{nihongo|Sanshi|三尸||qq=}}, entities believed to live inside the bodies of believers, from leaving during that night in order to report the deeds of believers to the god Tentei.
It is not known when this belief arrived in Japan, but it was widespread among the nobles of the imperial court by some time in the 9th century. The Japanese monk [[:en:Ennin|Ennin]], visiting [[:en:Tang dynasty|Tang China]] in 838, wrote that "This night no one sleeps. It is the same as New Year's Eve and the nights of ''Kōshin'' in our country."<ref>{{Cite book |last= |first= |url=http://archive.org/details/diaryrecordofpil0000enni |title=Ennin's Diary. The Record of a Pilgrimage to China in Search of the Law |title-link= |publisher=Ronald Press Company |year=1955 |location=New York |page=58 |translator-last=Reischauer |translator-first=Edwin O. |translator-link=Edwin O. Reischauer|qq=}}</ref> In the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]], [[:en:Bhikkhu|Buddhist monks]] started to write about Kōshin and spread the belief to a wider public. Numerous monuments or pillars called {{nihongo|Kōshin-tō|庚申塔||qq=}} (or also {{nihongo|Kōshin-zuka|庚申塚||qq=}}) were erected all over the country, and the belief remained very popular during the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. However, after the Meiji government issued the [[Shinbutsu bunri|Shinto and Buddhism Separation Order]] in 1872, Kōshin and other folk beliefs were officially rejected as superstitions.
Belief in Kōshin survives, although it is far less popular than it once was. Many Kōshin-tō have been moved inside Buddhist temples or private homes, but many remain alongside roads and there are still some well-maintained {{nihongo|Kōshin-dō|Kōshin-dō||qq=}} (Kōshin halls) either attached to Buddhist temples or standing alone.
==Deities and customs== The most ancient Kōshin custom is that of staying awake one special night every sixty days. This night is called ''Kōshin-Machi'' (庚申待 - Kōshin Waiting).
The main Kōshin belief is the concept that [[:en:Three Corpses|Three Corpses]], or ''Sanshi'' (三尸), live in every human body. The Sanshi keep track of the deeds of the person they inhabit. On the night called Kōshin-Machi, the ''Sanshis'' leave the body and go to [[:en:King of Heavens|Tentei]] (天帝), the Heavenly God, to report the deeds of that person. Tentei then punishes bad people, making them ill, shortening their lifespans or, in extreme cases, ending their lives. Believers in Kōshin try to live without performing bad deeds, but those who believe that they have reason to fear try to stay awake during Kōshin nights, as the only way to prevent the Sanshi from reporting to Tentei.
In the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]], Kōshin-Machi became more popular among commoners, leading to a proliferation of festivities and cultic activities. Many of these practices centered on the worship of specific deities. These deities were visualized in [[:en:Hanging scroll|Hanging scroll]]s, icons, and stone carvings, many of which continue to dot the rural landscape of Japan today. One specially prominent god in the Kōshin cult was [[Shōmen-Kongō]] (Blue-Faced [[:en:Vajra-Yakṣa|Vajra-Yakṣa]]), a fearsome deity with many arms. The first scriptures that established his connection with Kōshin were produced in the context of esoteric Buddhist rituals performed at the temple known as {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Onjōji|Onjōji]]|qq=}} or {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Miidera|Miidera]]|qq=}}. Another temple crucial in the early development of this cult was [[Shitennō-ji]]. Shōmen-Kongō became Kōshin-san when people expected this deity to make the Sanshis themselves ill and prevent them from going to Tentei.

== Years of Yang Metal Monkey == [[:en:Common Era|Common Era]] and [[:en:Japanese imperial year|Imperial Era]] designate years that are multiples of 60 as [[:en:Year|Year]] of Kōshin.
=== Nature and Era Change === Because both the heavenly stem and earthly branch of Kōshin are of [[:en:Metal|Metal]] nature, it was believed that the metal energy pervading the universe in a Kōshin year or day would render human hearts cold and unfeeling. The following combination, {{ill|Shinyuu|ja|1=Yin Metal Rooster|2=ja|辛酉|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinyuu|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, also being metal in nature—with Xin being of Yin energy—was thought to intensify this coldness. Consequently, Kōshin and Shinyuu were considered harbingers of political upheaval, and to avert such changes it was not uncommon to change eras for two consecutive years. For example, this occurred in the first years of [[:en:Man'en|Man'en]] ([[:en:1860|1860]]) and [[:en:Bunkyū|Bunkyu]] ([[:en:1861|1861]]).

Numerous monuments or pillars called {{nihongo|Kōshin-tō|庚申塔||qq=}} (or also {{nihongo|Kōshin-zuka|庚申塚||qq=}}) were erected all over the country, and the belief remained very popular during the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. However, after the Meiji government issued the [[Shinbutsu bunri|Shinto and Buddhism Separation Order]] in 1872, Kōshin and other folk beliefs were officially rejected as superstitions.
Belief in Kōshin survives, although it is far less popular than it once was. Many Kōshin-tō have been moved inside Buddhist temples or private homes, but many remain alongside roads and there are still some well-maintained {{nihongo|Kōshin-dō|Kōshin-dō||qq=}} (Kōshin halls) either attached to Buddhist temples or standing alone.
==Deities and customs== The most ancient Kōshin custom is that of staying awake one special night every sixty days. This night is called ''Kōshin-Machi'' (庚申待 - Kōshin Waiting).
The main Kōshin belief is the concept that [[:en:Three Corpses|Three Corpses]], or ''Sanshi'' (三尸), live in every human body. The Sanshi keep track of the deeds of the person they inhabit. On the night called Kōshin-Machi, the ''Sanshis'' leave the body and go to [[:en:King of Heavens|Tentei]] (天帝), the Heavenly God, to report the deeds of that person. Tentei then punishes bad people, making them ill, shortening their lifespans or, in extreme cases, ending their lives. Believers in Kōshin try to live without performing bad deeds, but those who believe that they have reason to fear try to stay awake during Kōshin nights, as the only way to prevent the Sanshi from reporting to Tentei.
In the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]], Kōshin-Machi became more popular among commoners, leading to a proliferation of festivities and cultic activities. Many of these practices centered on the worship of specific deities. These deities were visualized in [[:en:Hanging scroll|Hanging scroll]]s, icons, and stone carvings, many of which continue to dot the rural landscape of Japan today. One specially prominent god in the Kōshin cult was [[Shōmen-Kongō]] (Blue-Faced [[:en:Vajra-Yakṣa|Vajra-Yakṣa]]), a fearsome deity with many arms. The first scriptures that established his connection with Kōshin were produced in the context of esoteric Buddhist rituals performed at the temple known as {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Onjōji|Onjōji]]|qq=}} or {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Miidera|Miidera]]|qq=}}. Another temple crucial in the early development of this cult was [[Shitennō-ji]]. Shōmen-Kongō became Kōshin-san when people expected this deity to make the Sanshis themselves ill and prevent them from going to Tentei.

It is the 57th combination in the Sexagenary cycle comprehensive, preceded by {{ill|Kimi|ja|1=Yin Earth Goat|2=ja|己未|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} and followed by {{ill|Shinyuu|ja|1=Yin Metal Rooster|2=ja|辛酉|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinyuu|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. In {{ill|Yin-Yang Five Elements|ja|陰陽五行|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yin-Yang Five Elements|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 陰陽五行思想|1=yin-yang wu xing theory|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11265234}}, the stem {{ill|Geng|ja|庚|1=Kanoe (庚)|lt=Kanoe (庚)|2=ja|3=庚|4=zh|5=庚|1=Kanoe (庚)|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Geng|13=User:Immanuelle/Kanoe (庚)|qq=}} of the [[:en:Heavenly Stems|Ten Heavenly Stems]] represents Yang Metal, and the branch [[:en:Monkey (zodiac)|Monkey (申)]] of the [[:en:Earthly Branches|Twelve Earthly Branches]] also represents Yang Metal, a state referred to as {{ill|Bihwa|ja|五行思想#比和（ひわ）|1=Wu Xing|1=Wuxing (Chinese philosophy)#Harmonious Relationship (比和)|2=ja|3=五行思想#比和（ひわ）|lt=Harmonious Relationship (Five Elements)|qq=Bihwa|lt_ja=比和|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bihwa|13=User:Immanuelle/比和|qq=|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q218652}}.
==Pronunciation== * English: Yang Metal Monkey (庚申) ** Chinese (Mandarin Pinyin): gēngshēn ** Cantonese (Jyutping): gaang1 san1 ** Japanese: ***Kunyomi 1: Kanoe-saru ***Kunyomi 2: koukin-no-saru ***Onyomi 1: koushin ** Korean (Revised Romanization, Hangul): gyeongsin (경신) ** Vietnamese (Hán-Việt): Canh Thân
== Years of Yang Metal Monkey == [[:en:Common Era|Common Era]] and [[:en:Japanese imperial year|Imperial Era]] designate years that are multiples of 60 as [[:en:Year|Year]] of Kōshin.
=== Nature and Era Change === Because both the heavenly stem and earthly branch of Kōshin are of [[:en:Metal|Metal]] nature, it was believed that the metal energy pervading the universe in a Kōshin year or day would render human hearts cold and unfeeling. The following combination, {{ill|Shinyuu|ja|1=Yin Metal Rooster|2=ja|辛酉|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinyuu|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, also being metal in nature—with Xin being of Yin energy—was thought to intensify this coldness. Consequently, Kōshin and Shinyuu were considered harbingers of political upheaval, and to avert such changes it was not uncommon to change eras for two consecutive years. For example, this occurred in the first years of [[:en:Man'en|Man'en]] ([[:en:1860|1860]]) and [[:en:Bunkyū|Bunkyu]] ([[:en:1861|1861]]).

== Months of Yang Metal Monkey == In years where the last digit of the Western Calendar year is 3 or 8 (when the heavenly stem is {{ill|Guǐ|ja|癸|1=Mizunoto (癸)|lt=Mizunoto (癸)|2=ja|3=癸|4=zh|5=癸|1=Mizunoto (癸)|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Guǐ|13=User:Immanuelle/Mizunoto (癸)|qq=}} or {{ill|Wu|ja|戊|1=Tsuchinoe (戊)|lt=Tsuchinoe (戊)|2=ja|3=戊|4=zh|5=戊|1=Tsuchinoe (戊)|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Wu|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsuchinoe (戊)|qq=}}), the month of [[:en:July|July]] becomes the Kōshin [[:en:Month|Month (Calendar)]]. Note that here the month may refer either to a month of the {{ill|Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|ja|旧暦|1=Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|1=Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|11=Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|qq=}} or to a [[:en:Solar term|Solar term]] (from [[:en:Liqiu|Start of Autumn]] until the day before [[:en:Bailu (solar term)|White Dew]]).
== Days of Yang Metal Monkey ==
On Kōshin days, a Kōshin Vigil ({{ill|Kōshin Vigil|ja|庚申待|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōshin Vigil|qq=|1=Kōshin-machi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11486004}}, also known as {{ill|Kōshin Lecture|ja|庚申講|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōshin Lecture|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 庚申待|1=Kōshin-machi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11486004}}) was held. {{main|[[:en:Kōshin|Kōshin Faith]]|qq=}}
A Kōshin day is also the [[:en:Ennichi|Festival Day]] of [[:en:Śakra (Buddhism)|Taishakuten]].
=== Choosing a Day === Kōshin days occur on the sixth day (excluding intercalary days {{ill|Intercalary Day|ja|間日|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Intercalary Day|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) of the {{ill|Hassen|ja|八専|qq=|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hassen|qq=}} cycle. == See Also == * {{prefix|qq=}} * {{intitle|qq=}}

An event related to the belief is called {{nihongo|Kōshin-kō|庚申講||qq=}}, held on the Kōshin days that occur every 60 days in accordance with the [[:en:Chinese sexagenary cycle|Chinese sexagenary cycle]]. On this day some believers stay awake to prevent {{nihongo|Sanshi|三尸||qq=}}, entities believed to live inside the bodies of believers, from leaving during that night in order to report the deeds of believers to the god Tentei.
It is not known when this belief arrived in Japan, but it was widespread among the nobles of the imperial court by some time in the 9th century. The Japanese monk [[:en:Ennin|Ennin]], visiting [[:en:Tang dynasty|Tang China]] in 838, wrote that "This night no one sleeps. ==Pronunciation== * English: Yang Metal Monkey (庚申) ** Chinese (Mandarin Pinyin): gēngshēn ** Cantonese (Jyutping): gaang1 san1 ** Japanese: ***Kunyomi 1: Kanoe-saru ***Kunyomi 2: koukin-no-saru ***Onyomi 1: koushin ** Korean (Revised Romanization, Hangul): gyeongsin (경신) ** Vietnamese (Hán-Việt): Canh Thân
== Years of Yang Metal Monkey == [[:en:Common Era|Common Era]] and [[:en:Japanese imperial year|Imperial Era]] designate years that are multiples of 60 as [[:en:Year|Year]] of Kōshin.
=== Nature and Era Change === Because both the heavenly stem and earthly branch of Kōshin are of [[:en:Metal|Metal]] nature, it was believed that the metal energy pervading the universe in a Kōshin year or day would render human hearts cold and unfeeling. The following combination, {{ill|Shinyuu|ja|1=Yin Metal Rooster|2=ja|辛酉|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinyuu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, also being metal in nature—with Xin being of Yin energy—was thought to intensify this coldness. Consequently, Kōshin and Shinyuu were considered harbingers of political upheaval, and to avert such changes it was not uncommon to change eras for two consecutive years. For example, this occurred in the first years of [[:en:Man'en|Man'en]] ([[:en:1860|1860]]) and [[:en:Bunkyū|Bunkyu]] ([[:en:1861|1861]]).

== Months of Yang Metal Monkey == In years where the last digit of the Western Calendar year is 3 or 8 (when the heavenly stem is {{ill|Guǐ|ja|癸|1=Mizunoto (癸)|lt=Mizunoto (癸)|2=ja|3=癸|4=zh|5=癸|1=Mizunoto (癸)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Guǐ|13=User:Immanuelle/Mizunoto (癸)|qq=}} or {{ill|Wu|ja|戊|1=Tsuchinoe (戊)|lt=Tsuchinoe (戊)|2=ja|3=戊|4=zh|5=戊|1=Tsuchinoe (戊)|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Wu|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsuchinoe (戊)|qq=}}), the month of [[:en:July|July]] becomes the Kōshin [[:en:Month|Month (Calendar)]]. Note that here the month may refer either to a month of the {{ill|Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|ja|旧暦|1=Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|1=Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|11=Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|qq=}} or to a [[:en:Solar term|Solar term]] (from [[:en:Liqiu|Start of Autumn]] until the day before [[:en:Bailu (solar term)|White Dew]]).
== Days of Yang Metal Monkey ==
On Kōshin days, a Kōshin Vigil ({{ill|Kōshin Vigil|ja|庚申待|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōshin Vigil|1=Kōshin-machi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11486004}}, also known as {{ill|Kōshin Lecture|ja|庚申講|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōshin Lecture|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 庚申待|1=Kōshin-machi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11486004}}) was held. {{main|[[:en:Kōshin|Kōshin Faith]]|qq=}}
A Kōshin day is also the [[:en:Ennichi|Festival Day]] of [[:en:Śakra (Buddhism)|Taishakuten]].
=== Choosing a Day === Kōshin days occur on the sixth day (excluding intercalary days {{ill|Intercalary Day|ja|間日|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Intercalary Day|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) of the {{ill|Hassen|ja|八専|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hassen|qq=}} cycle. == See Also == * {{prefix|qq=}} * {{intitle|qq=}}

{{nihongo|'''''Kōshin'''''|庚申|1=Kōshin|lt=Yang Metal Monkey|2=ja|3=庚申|4=zh|5=庚申|6=ko|7=경신|lt_ko=경신|8=fr|9=Singe de métal|10=de|11=Metall-Affe||qq=}} or {{nihongo|''Kōshin-shinkō''|庚申信仰||qq=}} is a folk belief in [[:en:Japan|Japan]] with [[Taoism|Taoist]] origins, influenced by [[Shinto]], [[:en:Buddhism|Buddhism]] and other local beliefs.
An event related to the belief is called {{nihongo|Kōshin-kō|庚申講||qq=}}, held on the Kōshin days that occur every 60 days in accordance with the [[:en:Chinese sexagenary cycle|Chinese sexagenary cycle]]. On this day some believers stay awake to prevent {{nihongo|Sanshi|三尸||qq=}}, entities believed to live inside the bodies of believers, from leaving during that night in order to report the deeds of believers to the god Tentei.
It is not known when this belief arrived in Japan, but it was widespread among the nobles of the imperial court by some time in the 9th century. The Japanese monk [[:en:Ennin|Ennin]], visiting [[:en:Tang dynasty|Tang China]] in 838, wrote that "This night no one sleeps. It is the same as New Year's Eve and the nights of ''Kōshin'' in our country."<ref>{{Cite book |last= |first= |url=http://archive.org/details/diaryrecordofpil0000enni |title=Ennin's Diary. The Record of a Pilgrimage to China in Search of the Law |title-link= |publisher=Ronald Press Company |year=1955 |location=New York |page=58 |translator-last=Reischauer |translator-first=Edwin O. |translator-link=Edwin O. Reischauer|qq=}}</ref> In the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]], [[:en:Bhikkhu|Buddhist monks]] started to write about Kōshin and spread the belief to a wider public. Numerous monuments or pillars called {{nihongo|Kōshin-tō|庚申塔||qq=}} (or also {{nihongo|Kōshin-zuka|庚申塚||qq=}}) were erected all over the country, and the belief remained very popular during the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. However, after the Meiji government issued the [[Shinbutsu bunri|Shinto and Buddhism Separation Order]] in 1872, Kōshin and other folk beliefs were officially rejected as superstitions.
Belief in Kōshin survives, although it is far less popular than it once was. Many Kōshin-tō have been moved inside Buddhist temples or private homes, but many remain alongside roads and there are still some well-maintained {{nihongo|Kōshin-dō|Kōshin-dō||qq=}} (Kōshin halls) either attached to Buddhist temples or standing alone.
==Deities and customs== The most ancient Kōshin custom is that of staying awake one special night every sixty days. This night is called ''Kōshin-Machi'' (庚申待 - Kōshin Waiting).
The main Kōshin belief is the concept that [[:en:Three Corpses|Three Corpses]], or ''Sanshi'' (三尸), live in every human body. The Sanshi keep track of the deeds of the person they inhabit. On the night called Kōshin-Machi, the ''Sanshis'' leave the body and go to [[:en:King of Heavens|Tentei]] (天帝), the Heavenly God, to report the deeds of that person. Tentei then punishes bad people, making them ill, shortening their lifespans or, in extreme cases, ending their lives. Believers in Kōshin try to live without performing bad deeds, but those who believe that they have reason to fear try to stay awake during Kōshin nights, as the only way to prevent the Sanshi from reporting to Tentei.
In the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]], Kōshin-Machi became more popular among commoners, leading to a proliferation of festivities and cultic activities. Many of these practices centered on the worship of specific deities. These deities were visualized in [[:en:Hanging scroll|Hanging scroll]]s, icons, and stone carvings, many of which continue to dot the rural landscape of Japan today. One specially prominent god in the Kōshin cult was [[Shōmen-Kongō]] (Blue-Faced [[:en:Vajra-Yakṣa|Vajra-Yakṣa]]), a fearsome deity with many arms. The first scriptures that established his connection with Kōshin were produced in the context of esoteric Buddhist rituals performed at the temple known as {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Onjōji|Onjōji]]|qq=}} or {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Miidera|Miidera]]|qq=}}. Another temple crucial in the early development of this cult was [[Shitennō-ji]]. Shōmen-Kongō became Kōshin-san when people expected this deity to make the Sanshis themselves ill and prevent them from going to Tentei.

The following combination, {{ill|Shinyuu|ja|1=Yin Metal Rooster|2=ja|辛酉|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinyuu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, also being metal in nature—with Xin being of Yin energy—was thought to intensify this coldness. Consequently, Kōshin and Shinyuu were considered harbingers of political upheaval, and to avert such changes it was not uncommon to change eras for two consecutive years. For example, this occurred in the first years of [[:en:Man'en|Man'en]] ([[:en:1860|1860]]) and [[:en:Bunkyū|Bunkyu]] ([[:en:1861|1861]]).

== Months of Yang Metal Monkey == In years where the last digit of the Western Calendar year is 3 or 8 (when the heavenly stem is {{ill|Guǐ|ja|癸|1=Mizunoto (癸)|lt=Mizunoto (癸)|2=ja|3=癸|4=zh|5=癸|1=Mizunoto (癸)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Guǐ|13=User:Immanuelle/Mizunoto (癸)|qq=}} or {{ill|Wu|ja|戊|1=Tsuchinoe (戊)|lt=Tsuchinoe (戊)|2=ja|3=戊|4=zh|5=戊|1=Tsuchinoe (戊)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Wu|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsuchinoe (戊)|qq=}}), the month of [[:en:July|July]] becomes the Kōshin [[:en:Month|Month (Calendar)]]. Note that here the month may refer either to a month of the {{ill|Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|ja|旧暦|1=Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|1=Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|11=Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|qq=}} or to a [[:en:Solar term|Solar term]] (from [[:en:Liqiu|Start of Autumn]] until the day before [[:en:Bailu (solar term)|White Dew]]).
== Days of Yang Metal Monkey ==
On Kōshin days, a Kōshin Vigil ({{ill|Kōshin Vigil|ja|庚申待|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōshin Vigil|1=Kōshin-machi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11486004}}, also known as {{ill|Kōshin Lecture|ja|庚申講|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōshin Lecture|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 庚申待|1=Kōshin-machi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11486004}}) was held. {{main|[[:en:Kōshin|Kōshin Faith]]|qq=}}
A Kōshin day is also the [[:en:Ennichi|Festival Day]] of [[:en:Śakra (Buddhism)|Taishakuten]].
=== Choosing a Day === Kōshin days occur on the sixth day (excluding intercalary days {{ill|Intercalary Day|ja|間日|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Intercalary Day|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) of the {{ill|Hassen|ja|八専|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hassen|qq=}} cycle. == See Also == * {{prefix|qq=}} * {{intitle|qq=}}

{{nihongo|'''''Kōshin'''''|庚申|1=Kōshin|lt=Yang Metal Monkey|2=ja|3=庚申|4=zh|5=庚申|6=ko|7=경신|lt_ko=경신|8=fr|9=Singe de métal|10=de|11=Metall-Affe||qq=}} or {{nihongo|''Kōshin-shinkō''|庚申信仰||qq=}} is a folk belief in [[:en:Japan|Japan]] with [[Taoism|Taoist]] origins, influenced by [[Shinto]], [[:en:Buddhism|Buddhism]] and other local beliefs.
An event related to the belief is called {{nihongo|Kōshin-kō|庚申講||qq=}}, held on the Kōshin days that occur every 60 days in accordance with the [[:en:Chinese sexagenary cycle|Chinese sexagenary cycle]]. On this day some believers stay awake to prevent {{nihongo|Sanshi|三尸||qq=}}, entities believed to live inside the bodies of believers, from leaving during that night in order to report the deeds of believers to the god Tentei.
It is not known when this belief arrived in Japan, but it was widespread among the nobles of the imperial court by some time in the 9th century. The Japanese monk [[:en:Ennin|Ennin]], visiting [[:en:Tang dynasty|Tang China]] in 838, wrote that "This night no one sleeps. It is the same as New Year's Eve and the nights of ''Kōshin'' in our country."<ref>{{Cite book |last= |first= |url=http://archive.org/details/diaryrecordofpil0000enni |title=Ennin's Diary. The Record of a Pilgrimage to China in Search of the Law |title-link= |publisher=Ronald Press Company |year=1955 |location=New York |page=58 |translator-last=Reischauer |translator-first=Edwin O. |translator-link=Edwin O. Reischauer|qq=}}</ref> In the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]], [[:en:Bhikkhu|Buddhist monks]] started to write about Kōshin and spread the belief to a wider public. Numerous monuments or pillars called {{nihongo|Kōshin-tō|庚申塔||qq=}} (or also {{nihongo|Kōshin-zuka|庚申塚||qq=}}) were erected all over the country, and the belief remained very popular during the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. However, after the Meiji government issued the [[Shinbutsu bunri|Shinto and Buddhism Separation Order]] in 1872, Kōshin and other folk beliefs were officially rejected as superstitions.
Belief in Kōshin survives, although it is far less popular than it once was. Many Kōshin-tō have been moved inside Buddhist temples or private homes, but many remain alongside roads and there are still some well-maintained {{nihongo|Kōshin-dō|Kōshin-dō||qq=}} (Kōshin halls) either attached to Buddhist temples or standing alone.
==Deities and customs== The most ancient Kōshin custom is that of staying awake one special night every sixty days. This night is called ''Kōshin-Machi'' (庚申待 - Kōshin Waiting).
The main Kōshin belief is the concept that [[:en:Three Corpses|Three Corpses]], or ''Sanshi'' (三尸), live in every human body. The Sanshi keep track of the deeds of the person they inhabit. On the night called Kōshin-Machi, the ''Sanshis'' leave the body and go to [[:en:King of Heavens|Tentei]] (天帝), the Heavenly God, to report the deeds of that person. Tentei then punishes bad people, making them ill, shortening their lifespans or, in extreme cases, ending their lives. Believers in Kōshin try to live without performing bad deeds, but those who believe that they have reason to fear try to stay awake during Kōshin nights, as the only way to prevent the Sanshi from reporting to Tentei.
In the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]], Kōshin-Machi became more popular among commoners, leading to a proliferation of festivities and cultic activities. Many of these practices centered on the worship of specific deities. These deities were visualized in [[:en:Hanging scroll|Hanging scroll]]s, icons, and stone carvings, many of which continue to dot the rural landscape of Japan today. One specially prominent god in the Kōshin cult was [[Shōmen-Kongō]] (Blue-Faced [[:en:Vajra-Yakṣa|Vajra-Yakṣa]]), a fearsome deity with many arms. The first scriptures that established his connection with Kōshin were produced in the context of esoteric Buddhist rituals performed at the temple known as {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Onjōji|Onjōji]]|qq=}} or {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Miidera|Miidera]]|qq=}}. Another temple crucial in the early development of this cult was [[Shitennō-ji]]. Shōmen-Kongō became Kōshin-san when people expected this deity to make the Sanshis themselves ill and prevent them from going to Tentei.

== Months of Yang Metal Monkey == In years where the last digit of the Western Calendar year is 3 or 8 (when the heavenly stem is {{ill|Guǐ|ja|癸|1=Mizunoto (癸)|lt=Mizunoto (癸)|2=ja|3=癸|4=zh|5=癸|1=Mizunoto (癸)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Guǐ|13=User:Immanuelle/Mizunoto (癸)|qq=}} or {{ill|Wu|ja|戊|1=Tsuchinoe (戊)|lt=Tsuchinoe (戊)|2=ja|3=戊|4=zh|5=戊|1=Tsuchinoe (戊)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Wu|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsuchinoe (戊)|qq=}}), the month of [[:en:July|July]] becomes the Kōshin [[:en:Month|Month (Calendar)]]. Note that here the month may refer either to a month of the {{ill|Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|ja|旧暦|1=Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|1=Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|11=Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|qq=}} or to a [[:en:Solar term|Solar term]] (from [[:en:Liqiu|Start of Autumn]] until the day before [[:en:Bailu (solar term)|White Dew]]).
== Days of Yang Metal Monkey ==
On Kōshin days, a Kōshin Vigil ({{ill|Kōshin Vigil|ja|庚申待|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōshin Vigil|1=Kōshin-machi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11486004}}, also known as {{ill|Kōshin Lecture|ja|庚申講|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōshin Lecture|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 庚申待|1=Kōshin-machi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11486004}}) was held. {{main|[[:en:Kōshin|Kōshin Faith]]|qq=}}
A Kōshin day is also the [[:en:Ennichi|Festival Day]] of [[:en:Śakra (Buddhism)|Taishakuten]].
=== Choosing a Day === Kōshin days occur on the sixth day (excluding intercalary days {{ill|Intercalary Day|ja|間日|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Intercalary Day|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) of the {{ill|Hassen|ja|八専|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hassen|qq=}} cycle. == See Also == * {{prefix|qq=}} * {{intitle|qq=}}

{{nihongo|'''''Kōshin'''''|庚申|1=Kōshin|lt=Yang Metal Monkey|2=ja|3=庚申|4=zh|5=庚申|6=ko|7=경신|lt_ko=경신|8=fr|9=Singe de métal|10=de|11=Metall-Affe||qq=}} or {{nihongo|''Kōshin-shinkō''|庚申信仰||qq=}} is a folk belief in [[:en:Japan|Japan]] with [[Taoism|Taoist]] origins, influenced by [[Shinto]], [[:en:Buddhism|Buddhism]] and other local beliefs.
An event related to the belief is called {{nihongo|Kōshin-kō|庚申講||qq=}}, held on the Kōshin days that occur every 60 days in accordance with the [[:en:Chinese sexagenary cycle|Chinese sexagenary cycle]]. On this day some believers stay awake to prevent {{nihongo|Sanshi|三尸||qq=}}, entities believed to live inside the bodies of believers, from leaving during that night in order to report the deeds of believers to the god Tentei.
It is not known when this belief arrived in Japan, but it was widespread among the nobles of the imperial court by some time in the 9th century. The Japanese monk [[:en:Ennin|Ennin]], visiting [[:en:Tang dynasty|Tang China]] in 838, wrote that "This night no one sleeps. It is the same as New Year's Eve and the nights of ''Kōshin'' in our country."<ref>{{Cite book |last= |first= |url=http://archive.org/details/diaryrecordofpil0000enni |title=Ennin's Diary. The Record of a Pilgrimage to China in Search of the Law |title-link= |publisher=Ronald Press Company |year=1955 |location=New York |page=58 |translator-last=Reischauer |translator-first=Edwin O. |translator-link=Edwin O. Reischauer|qq=}}</ref> In the [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]], [[:en:Bhikkhu|Buddhist monks]] started to write about Kōshin and spread the belief to a wider public. Numerous monuments or pillars called {{nihongo|Kōshin-tō|庚申塔||qq=}} (or also {{nihongo|Kōshin-zuka|庚申塚||qq=}}) were erected all over the country, and the belief remained very popular during the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. However, after the Meiji government issued the [[Shinbutsu bunri|Shinto and Buddhism Separation Order]] in 1872, Kōshin and other folk beliefs were officially rejected as superstitions.
Belief in Kōshin survives, although it is far less popular than it once was. Many Kōshin-tō have been moved inside Buddhist temples or private homes, but many remain alongside roads and there are still some well-maintained {{nihongo|Kōshin-dō|Kōshin-dō||qq=}} (Kōshin halls) either attached to Buddhist temples or standing alone.
==Deities and customs== The most ancient Kōshin custom is that of staying awake one special night every sixty days. This night is called ''Kōshin-Machi'' (庚申待 - Kōshin Waiting).
The main Kōshin belief is the concept that [[:en:Three Corpses|Three Corpses]], or ''Sanshi'' (三尸), live in every human body. The Sanshi keep track of the deeds of the person they inhabit. On the night called Kōshin-Machi, the ''Sanshis'' leave the body and go to [[:en:King of Heavens|Tentei]] (天帝), the Heavenly God, to report the deeds of that person. Tentei then punishes bad people, making them ill, shortening their lifespans or, in extreme cases, ending their lives. Believers in Kōshin try to live without performing bad deeds, but those who believe that they have reason to fear try to stay awake during Kōshin nights, as the only way to prevent the Sanshi from reporting to Tentei.
In the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]], Kōshin-Machi became more popular among commoners, leading to a proliferation of festivities and cultic activities. Many of these practices centered on the worship of specific deities. These deities were visualized in [[:en:Hanging scroll|Hanging scroll]]s, icons, and stone carvings, many of which continue to dot the rural landscape of Japan today. One specially prominent god in the Kōshin cult was [[Shōmen-Kongō]] (Blue-Faced [[:en:Vajra-Yakṣa|Vajra-Yakṣa]]), a fearsome deity with many arms. The first scriptures that established his connection with Kōshin were produced in the context of esoteric Buddhist rituals performed at the temple known as {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Onjōji|Onjōji]]|qq=}} or {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Miidera|Miidera]]|qq=}}. Another temple crucial in the early development of this cult was [[Shitennō-ji]]. Shōmen-Kongō became Kōshin-san when people expected this deity to make the Sanshis themselves ill and prevent them from going to Tentei.

It is the 57th combination in the Sexagenary cycle comprehensive, preceded by {{ill|Kimi|ja|1=Yin Earth Goat|2=ja|己未|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimi|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} and followed by {{ill|Shinyuu|ja|1=Yin Metal Rooster|2=ja|辛酉|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinyuu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. In {{ill|Yin-Yang Five Elements|ja|陰陽五行|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yin-Yang Five Elements|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 陰陽五行思想|1=yin-yang wu xing theory|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11265234}}, the stem {{ill|Geng|ja|庚|1=Kanoe (庚)|lt=Kanoe (庚)|2=ja|3=庚|4=zh|5=庚|1=Kanoe (庚)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Geng|13=User:Immanuelle/Kanoe (庚)|qq=}} of the [[:en:Heavenly Stems|Ten Heavenly Stems]] represents Yang Metal, and the branch [[:en:Monkey (zodiac)|Monkey (申)]] of the [[:en:Earthly Branches|Twelve Earthly Branches]] also represents Yang Metal, a state referred to as {{ill|Bihwa|ja|五行思想#比和（ひわ）|1=Wu Xing|1=Wuxing (Chinese philosophy)#Harmonious Relationship (比和)|2=ja|3=五行思想#比和（ひわ）|lt=Harmonious Relationship (Five Elements)|qq=Bihwa|lt_ja=比和|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bihwa|13=User:Immanuelle/比和|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q218652}}.
==Pronunciation== * English: Yang Metal Monkey (庚申) ** Chinese (Mandarin Pinyin): gēngshēn ** Cantonese (Jyutping): gaang1 san1 ** Japanese: ***Kunyomi 1: Kanoe-saru ***Kunyomi 2: koukin-no-saru ***Onyomi 1: koushin ** Korean (Revised Romanization, Hangul): gyeongsin (경신) ** Vietnamese (Hán-Việt): Canh Thân
== Years of Yang Metal Monkey == [[:en:Common Era|Common Era]] and [[:en:Japanese imperial year|Imperial Era]] designate years that are multiples of 60 as [[:en:Year|Year]] of Kōshin.
=== Nature and Era Change === Because both the heavenly stem and earthly branch of Kōshin are of [[:en:Metal|Metal]] nature, it was believed that the metal energy pervading the universe in a Kōshin year or day would render human hearts cold and unfeeling. The following combination, {{ill|Shinyuu|ja|1=Yin Metal Rooster|2=ja|辛酉|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinyuu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, also being metal in nature—with Xin being of Yin energy—was thought to intensify this coldness. Consequently, Kōshin and Shinyuu were considered harbingers of political upheaval, and to avert such changes it was not uncommon to change eras for two consecutive years. For example, this occurred in the first years of [[:en:Man'en|Man'en]] ([[:en:1860|1860]]) and [[:en:Bunkyū|Bunkyu]] ([[:en:1861|1861]]).

The main Kōshin belief is the concept that [[:en:Three Corpses|Three Corpses]], or ''Sanshi'' (三尸), live in every human body. The Sanshi keep track of the deeds of the person they inhabit. On the night called Kōshin-Machi, the ''Sanshis'' leave the body and go to [[:en:King of Heavens|Tentei]] (天帝), the Heavenly God, to report the deeds of that person. Tentei then punishes bad people, making them ill, shortening their lifespans or, in extreme cases, ending their lives. Believers in Kōshin try to live without performing bad deeds, but those who believe that they have reason to fear try to stay awake during Kōshin nights, as the only way to prevent the Sanshi from reporting to Tentei.
In the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]], Kōshin-Machi became more popular among commoners, leading to a proliferation of festivities and cultic activities. Many of these practices centered on the worship of specific deities. These deities were visualized in [[:en:Hanging scroll|Hanging scroll]]s, icons, and stone carvings, many of which continue to dot the rural landscape of Japan today. One specially prominent god in the Kōshin cult was [[Shōmen-Kongō]] (Blue-Faced [[:en:Vajra-Yakṣa|Vajra-Yakṣa]]), a fearsome deity with many arms. The first scriptures that established his connection with Kōshin were produced in the context of esoteric Buddhist rituals performed at the temple known as {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Onjōji|Onjōji]]|qq=}} or {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Miidera|Miidera]]|qq=}}. Another temple crucial in the early development of this cult was [[Shitennō-ji]]. Shōmen-Kongō became Kōshin-san when people expected this deity to make the Sanshis themselves ill and prevent them from going to Tentei.

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[af:Metaalaap (astrologie)]][[cdo:Gĕng-sĭng]][[de:Metall-Affe]][[en:Metal Monkey]][[fr:Singe de métal]][[hak:Kâng-sṳ̂n]][[ja:庚申]][[ko:경신]][[vi:Canh Thân]][[za:Gengsaen]][[zh-min-nan:Keng-sin]][[zh-yue:庚申]][[zh:庚申]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q3082157]] Wikidata name: Kōshin [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 07:49, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{infobox Chinese|l=Yang Metal Monkey|kanji=庚申|romaji=kanoe saru|onyomi=kōshin|p=gēngshēn|w=keng-shen|mi=kɤŋ⁵³ ʂən|y=geng1 san1|j=geng1 san1|ci=kɪŋ ʂɐn|mc=kæŋ ʂin|oc-bs=kˤraŋ ʂin|qq=}} {{otheruses|Sexagenary cycle|日本人の信仰対象|庚申信仰|qq=}} {{merge|1=Kōshin|qq=}} Might be worth moving to or merging with {{ill|Kōshin|ja|こうしん|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōshin|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} {{afc comment|1=This one is really weird with a potential wikidata conflict[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 19:32, 10 November 2025 (UTC)}} {{Sexagenary cycle comprehensive|qq=}} '''Yang Metal Monkey also known as Kōshin''' (庚申; かのえさる、こうきんのさる、こうしん) is one of the [[:en:Sexagenary cycle|Sexagenary cycle]].
It is the 57th combination in the Sexagenary cycle comprehensive, preceded by {{ill|Kimi|ja|1=Yin Earth Goat|2=ja|己未|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kimi|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} and followed by {{ill|Shinyuu|ja|1=Yin Metal Rooster|2=ja|辛酉|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinyuu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}. In {{ill|Yin-Yang Five Elements|ja|陰陽五行|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yin-Yang Five Elements|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 陰陽五行思想|1=yin-yang wu xing theory|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11265234}}, the stem {{ill|Geng|ja|庚|1=Kanoe (庚)|lt=Kanoe (庚)|2=ja|3=庚|4=zh|5=庚|1=Kanoe (庚)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Geng|13=User:Immanuelle/Kanoe (庚)|qq=}} of the [[:en:Heavenly Stems|Ten Heavenly Stems]] represents Yang Metal, and the branch [[:en:Monkey (zodiac)|Monkey (申)]] of the [[:en:Earthly Branches|Twelve Earthly Branches]] also represents Yang Metal, a state referred to as {{ill|Bihwa|ja|五行思想#比和（ひわ）|1=Wu Xing|1=Wuxing (Chinese philosophy)#Harmonious Relationship (比和)|2=ja|3=五行思想#比和（ひわ）|lt=Harmonious Relationship (Five Elements)|qq=Bihwa|lt_ja=比和|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Bihwa|13=User:Immanuelle/比和|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q218652}}.
==Pronunciation== * English: Yang Metal Monkey (庚申) ** Chinese (Mandarin Pinyin): gēngshēn ** Cantonese (Jyutping): gaang1 san1 ** Japanese: ***Kunyomi 1: Kanoe-saru ***Kunyomi 2: koukin-no-saru ***Onyomi 1: koushin ** Korean (Revised Romanization, Hangul): gyeongsin (경신) ** Vietnamese (Hán-Việt): Canh Thân
== Years of Yang Metal Monkey == [[:en:Common Era|Common Era]] and [[:en:Japanese imperial year|Imperial Era]] designate years that are multiples of 60 as [[:en:Year|Year]] of Kōshin.
=== Nature and Era Change === Because both the heavenly stem and earthly branch of Kōshin are of [[:en:Metal|Metal]] nature, it was believed that the metal energy pervading the universe in a Kōshin year or day would render human hearts cold and unfeeling. The following combination, {{ill|Shinyuu|ja|1=Yin Metal Rooster|2=ja|辛酉|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinyuu|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, also being metal in nature—with Xin being of Yin energy—was thought to intensify this coldness. Consequently, Kōshin and Shinyuu were considered harbingers of political upheaval, and to avert such changes it was not uncommon to change eras for two consecutive years. For example, this occurred in the first years of [[:en:Man'en|Man'en]] ([[:en:1860|1860]]) and [[:en:Bunkyū|Bunkyu]] ([[:en:1861|1861]]).

== Months of Yang Metal Monkey == In years where the last digit of the Western Calendar year is 3 or 8 (when the heavenly stem is {{ill|Guǐ|ja|癸|1=Mizunoto (癸)|lt=Mizunoto (癸)|2=ja|3=癸|4=zh|5=癸|1=Mizunoto (癸)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Guǐ|13=User:Immanuelle/Mizunoto (癸)|qq=}} or {{ill|Wu|ja|戊|1=Tsuchinoe (戊)|lt=Tsuchinoe (戊)|2=ja|3=戊|4=zh|5=戊|1=Tsuchinoe (戊)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Wu|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsuchinoe (戊)|qq=}}), the month of [[:en:July|July]] becomes the Kōshin [[:en:Month|Month (Calendar)]]. Note that here the month may refer either to a month of the {{ill|Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|ja|旧暦|1=Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|1=Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|11=Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|13=User:Immanuelle/Japanese Lunisolar Calendar|qq=}} or to a [[:en:Solar term|Solar term]] (from [[:en:Liqiu|Start of Autumn]] until the day before [[:en:Bailu (solar term)|White Dew]]).
== Days of Yang Metal Monkey ==
On Kōshin days, a Kōshin Vigil ({{ill|Kōshin Vigil|ja|庚申待|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōshin Vigil|1=Kōshin-machi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11486004}}, also known as {{ill|Kōshin Lecture|ja|庚申講|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōshin Lecture|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 庚申待|1=Kōshin-machi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11486004}}) was held. {{main|[[:en:Kōshin|Kōshin Faith]]|qq=}}
A Kōshin day is also the [[:en:Ennichi|Festival Day]] of [[:en:Śakra (Buddhism)|Taishakuten]].
=== Choosing a Day === Kōshin days occur on the sixth day (excluding intercalary days {{ill|Intercalary Day|ja|間日|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Intercalary Day|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) of the {{ill|Hassen|ja|八専|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hassen|qq=}} cycle. == See Also == * {{prefix|qq=}} * {{intitle|qq=}}
